desc:
In the inorder sequence of a binary tree (left subtree, node, right subtree) the successor of a node is the node that comes right after it. Note that the tree is an ordinary binary tree, not a search tree, so values are not sorted.

All node values of tree are distinct. For every value q in queries (each of them is the value of some node in the tree) report the value of the inorder successor of that node, or -1 if the node is the last one in inorder. Return the answers in the order of the queries; the same value may be queried several times.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [5, 8, 2, 7, -1, 4, 9] the inorder sequence is 7, 8, 5, 4, 2, 9. For queries = [8, 9, 4] the answer is [5, -1, 2].
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 10,000, and all node values are distinct
Every query value occurs in the tree
The tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: In a search tree you could use ordering to find a successor. Here you cannot: the structure of the tree is all you have.
The successor of a node is simply the next element of the inorder sequence, so one traversal gives the answer for every node at once.
Compute the inorder sequence once (iteratively), store next[value] for consecutive pairs (and -1 for the last one), then answer each query by a lookup.
editorial: For a single query you could reason locally: if the node has a right subtree the successor is the leftmost node of that subtree; otherwise it is the nearest ancestor of which the node lies in the left subtree. That needs parent pointers or a root-to-node path. With many queries it is simpler and faster to produce the whole inorder sequence once.

Run the iterative inorder traversal, remember the previous value, and fill a dictionary succ[prev] = current for every consecutive pair. The last value gets -1. Because values are distinct the dictionary is unambiguous, and every query becomes a constant-time lookup. Total O(n + q) time and O(n) space.
